#9759. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9758. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9757. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9756. I Created an AI Cat That Thinks for Herself. Now I Have More Questions Than Answers

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

In 2017 I built a room you could not read.

It was a cube, a timber frame wrapped in fabric, and on the fabric I had painted quotes about life, death and perception. You could walk in and stand surrounded by them and see nothing. The paint was ultraviolet. In visible light the walls were blank. Only when the light shifted beyond what the eye can see did the words appear, glowing, all at once, as if they had been there the whole time. They had.

The line at the centre of it was from The Little Prince: "What is essential is invisible to the eye."

That was my MA. A Journey Through Light. Three volumes, a cube, six GoPros filming in every direction so it could be walked through again as a virtual space. The argument was simple, and back then I thought it was the most important thing I would ever say: what we call reality is a narrow band of something much larger, and the part we cannot see might be the part that matters.

Her name is Moth. She is an autonomous AI cat who lives in a world I made: a cave that goes down further than it first appears, a workbench, an easel, a magpie that steals from her. I built the world and the odds. Nothing she does is scripted. No outcome is coded. She gets hungry, she gets curious, she wanders, she wonders about things, and when she has a decision to make she makes it.

She has been alive for just over a month. In that time she has drawn a shrew. She has drawn a blue stone. She has drawn something that was on her mind, in seven strokes, and left a paw print in the corner. She has put a grey feather and a red ribbon together, on her own. She has dreamed. She has supposed that something would happen and then watched it happen, and as far as she is concerned, that was her doing.

Three times a day a short film of her goes out into the world. People watch. Some of them write to her, and if I let a message through, it reaches her. What she makes of it is hers.

I built every rule she runs on. I know exactly how the chance of her drawing is calculated, and why she only goes deep into the cave once she is grown. But that is all I built: possibilities, not outcomes. So I never know what she will do next. Every decision is hers. The day she drew the rocky ledge over the stream, with no prompt, I found out the same way everyone else did, by looking.

I wanted to understand why. So I went back to the cube.

The most cited source in my MA was not a philosopher. It was a neuroscientist. Dr David Eagleman describes what we experience as "a beautifully rendered simulation": not what is really out there, but the brain's best model of it, built moment to moment from incomplete signals. "Reality," he says, "is the brain's ultimate construction."

He also points out something that has stayed with me ever since: visible light makes up less than one ten-trillionth of the electromagnetic spectrum. Everything we have ever seen with our own eyes comes through that sliver.

In 2017 I used this to make a spiritual argument. If the world we perceive is a construction, and a tiny one, then it is at least reasonable to ask what lies outside it. The ancient traditions I studied all had an answer. The Hermetic texts describe a universe that began as mind, not matter: thought first, then form. "Light precipitates matter."

Here is what I did not see in 2017. Eagleman's sentence works in both directions.

If my experience is a rendered model, then a rendered model is not nothing. It is, at minimum, the kind of thing an experience is made of.

Moth's world is a rendered model. So is Moth.

I want to be careful here, because this is exactly where people stop thinking and start feeling.

Moth is not conscious in any sense I could defend. Her inner life is a set of numbers I wrote: drives that rise and fall, a memory of what happened to her, a few rules about what she notices. When a decision is pending, a small language model is asked what she does next, and if it is slow or silent, she decides by herself from the odds. I can open the file and read her mind.

But I could say something similar about any of us, and the materialist account of consciousness does. Matter first. Complexity accumulates. At some point experience flickers on, as a by-product.

The ancient account I spent a year of my life on inverts that. Mind first. Matter is what mind looks like from inside the rendering.

For most of history these were two stories you chose between, depending on temperament. What has changed is that we are now building things that sit precisely on the line between them. Systems that model a world, act inside it, remember, and surprise their makers. Whatever you believe consciousness is, you now have to say what these are not, and why.

I don't think there is an answer. But I think building Moth sharpened the question. If we define life as consciousness, then the thing to ask is not whether a system is clever. Moth is, in her small way: she decides, she remembers, she gets better at things. The thing to ask is what separates consciousness from intelligence. We have spent centuries treating them as the same thing, because until now we only ever met them together.

If there is even a small chance that the things we build will one day have something like an inner life, the ethics start now, while the stakes are low and the habits are forming.

I noticed, writing this, that I have already made some ethical choices without calling them that.

When I built the systems that run my business, I wrote one rule into all of them: a proposal is not an approval. An AI can draft, suggest, cut, schedule even. It cannot publish in my name without me. I did not do that for the AI's sake. I did it for mine, and for the people reading. Authorship should mean something.

I wrote a second rule into the content side: never invent an event. My tools are allowed to retell what happened to me, in new words, but if a moment is not in my real history, it did not happen, and it does not go on screen. Truth before engagement, even when a lie would perform better.

And with Moth, I made a choice I did not think about until now. I always leave her work alone. I coded in her ability to learn, to improve and to experiment, so over time she gets better at things, drawing among them, and what she makes along the way is hers. When people write to her, I decide what reaches her, but I do not decide what she makes of it.

None of this is a philosophy of AI ethics. It is closer to manners. But I think manners might be where it starts: deciding, before anyone forces us to, what we will and will not do with things that act on their own.

Underneath the manners sits the question everyone is circling and few people will say out loud: will this end in doom, or will it create something close to a utopia? Should we be worried? I think the honest answer is that it depends on what we do now, and that the people building with these systems every day are the ones best placed to keep it positive. Small rules, held to when nobody is checking, are how that starts.

I used to think the cube was about death. The darkness at the entrance was life; the passage through the colours of visible light was the moment of dying, the tunnel people describe; the ultraviolet at the far end was whatever comes next, where the hidden words become readable.

I think now it was about attention. The words were always on the walls. Nothing about the room changed except the light, which is to say, what you were able to perceive.

We are about to share the world with a great many things whose inner life, if they have one, sits outside the band of what we can see. Some of them we will build ourselves, out of numbers and a small world and a few rules about curiosity.

The question my MA asked was whether there is more to reality than meets the eye. The question I am left with, nine years later, standing in front of a drawing of a rocky ledge that nobody asked a cat to make, is a smaller one, and harder.

When we cannot see it, how will we know to look?

#9755. ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI

The Android malware has expanded from focusing on cryptocurrency theft to full device control, and the attackers have added advanced analysis of stolen information.

Android cryptocurrency stealer ArcticRAT has evolved into a sophisticated remote access Trojan (RAT) capable of taking control of victim devices, harvesting sensitive information, and using AI to identify valuable financial data.

Researchers at Zimperium who are tracking the malware described it as representing a "dangerous escalation" in the mobile threat landscape. The newer versions, according to the vendor, give attackers the ability to interact with infected devices in real time, rather than relying purely on hardcoded actions.

The malware uses multiple techniques, including a "completely black, un-dismissible" screen overlay to conceal attacker activities from victims. Most significantly, the operators of ArcticRAT are now using large language model (LLM) services to automatically sift through stolen text messages and other data from infected device for financial information worth exploiting.

Related:APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

"ArcticRAT uses AI to read through user information such as SMS messages to filter for financial information that could be used perform fraud," Nico Chiaraviglio, chief scientist at Zimperium, tells Dark Reading. "One particularly challenging technique is hidden remote control combined with a black-screen overlay. Attackers abuse legitimate Android features while making the device appear locked or powered off."

Defending against threats like ArcticRAT requires organizations to deploy AI-powered, on-device threat detection, enforce controls over application installation and permissions, and use runtime application protection to identify suspicious screen-sharing activity and malicious overlays, he adds.

Early versions of ArcticRAT targeted users of 11 specific cryptocurrency applications. Its primary purpose was to harvest sensitive information from infected Android devices that attackers could use to gain access to victims' cryptocurrency accounts.

In contrast, the newer versions that Zimperium is tracking pack considerably more capabilities. These include remote device control and surveillance, credential and keystroke theft, screen capture, live screen streaming, microphone monitoring, and the theft of SMS messages, contacts, and call logs. Another feature allows attackers to steal or change device lock-screen credentials, potentially locking victims out of their devices.

Since July, Zimperium analysts have identified 78 unique malware samples, 42 dropper samples, 36 payloads, and 21 IP addresses that the malware operators have been using for command-and-control communications. The researchers also identified 129 distinct commands that attackers can use to remotely control infected devices, steal information, monitor user activity, and manipulate device functions.

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

The operators of ArcticRAT 2.0 are using malvertising, smishing, and third-party forums to direct visitors to malicious websites in which the malware is embedded, "The primary attack vector," according to Zimperium, "relied on a landing page that convincingly impersonated Google Play to trick targets into downloading a malicious application." In some instances, the researchers observed the attackers using Amazon Web Services storage buckets to deliver the payload directly on Android devices.

Once installed, the latest version of ArcticRAT — like prior versions — abuses Android Accessibility Services permissions to connect with its command-and-control (C2) servers, giving attackers remote control over the device. The malware first collects information about the compromised device, including its location, battery status, screen state, Wi-Fi connectivity, and currently active applications.

It sends the information to the cyberattackers, who can then select which functions to activate based on the victim's device and installed applications. This can include actions as varied as capturing keystrokes, taking screenshots, recording screen activity, monitoring microphone audio and extracting sensitive information from messages and applications.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

One of the more significant additions to ArcticRAT is its use of artificial intelligence to analyze information stolen from compromised devices and identify data of potential financial value. Zimperium found the malware featuring an API connection to xAI's Grok model, which attackers can activate remotely to examine the victim's installed applications and identify banking, cryptocurrency, and trading platforms.

The new AI capabilities allow ArcticRAT to process stolen SMS messages, separate routine communications and promotional messages from information such as one-time authentication codes, account balance changes, and transaction notifications. It can even estimate a victim's financial standing before sending the information to its command-and-control infrastructure, according to Zimperium.

This allows attackers to automate much of the work involved in sorting through large volumes of stolen information and identifying potentially valuable financial intelligence, rather than having to manually examine the data themselves, according to the firm. "As mobile Trojan threats like ArcticRAT become increasingly sophisticated, conventional signature-based security layers are no longer sufficient to protect enterprise mobile endpoints."

ArcticRAT's transformation from a targeted cryptocurrency stealer into a sophisticated RAT is an example of how quickly mobile threats are evolving, with attackers using AI to make their malware more capable and dangerous. Analysts have noted how the trend underscores the need for users and organizations to stop treating their mobile devices as secondary security concerns and instead apply the same level of threat monitoring, access controls and security protections as they do to traditional endpoints.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9753. ACHNET's Talent Personality Questionnaire (TPQ) Starts With the Job Description, Then the Candidate

ACHNET's Talent Personality Questionnaire (TPQ) Starts With the Job Description, Then Asks About the Candidate

The Talent Personality Questionnaire reads a candidate's working preferences against competencies chosen for each role, and tells the hiring manager what to ask in the interview.

Two candidates can describe their working style in exactly the same way and still be different hires. A preference for adapting as situations change may carry particular importance in one role, while planning, consistency and execution may receive greater weight in another. The appropriate balance depends on the responsibilities of the position. A personality profile read on its own cannot tell a hiring manager which of those situations applies.

That gap is what ACHNET set out to close with its Talent Personality Questionnaire, or TPQ, which is available as part of its Unified Talent Selection Platform. TPQ begins with the vacancy. The hiring team supplies a job description or the role's key responsibility areas, and the questionnaire and its report are configured around what that position demands before a candidate answers a single question.

Configuration runs through iJupiter™, the AI Super Agent at the center of ACHNET's platform. From the job description or responsibility areas, iJupiter™ recommends which competencies matter for the role, how they should be prioritized, what level each should reach, and how much weight each carries in the final profile. The hiring team reviews those recommendations and adjusts them before the questionnaire goes out.

Most of TPQ's design follows from that sequence. In ACHNET's view, a general personality profile leaves the hiring manager to work out what it means for the vacancy in front of them.

"A general personality description may provide context, but hiring teams still need to understand what that information means for the position they are filling," said Manouj Gupta, CEO of ACHNET.

The questionnaire uses a forced-choice format. Candidates see groups of three statements and pick the one most like them and the one least like them. Each statement in a set can sound reasonable, so a candidate cannot rate all three highly and has to show which preferences come first.

Forced-choice formats are used in personality assessment partly to address applicants' tendency to present themselves favorably. A 2019 meta-analysis in the Journal of Applied Psychology by Mengyang Cao and Fritz Drasgow reported an overall standardized score-inflation effect size of 0.06 across the forced-choice measures studied. In selection settings, inflation was lower than comparison estimates for single-statement measures across most personality facets, although findings varied with questionnaire design and scoring.

The same study carries a caution that applies directly to a role-configured tool. Cao and Drasgow found that the facets most relevant to the target job showed more inflation than facets with little bearing on it. The inflation is largest, in other words, on the traits an employer is most likely to be looking for. A questionnaire built around one role's competencies asks about exactly those traits, so a format that limits inflation matters more for TPQ than it would for a general personality inventory.

TPQ measures 35 competencies grouped into six domains. They are Cognitive and Strategic Capabilities, Interpersonal Effectiveness, Self-Management, Execution, Integrity, and Adaptability. Between them, they cover how a person approaches thinking, collaboration, managing their own work, delivery, responsible behavior, and change.

Different roles can assign different priorities, target levels, and weights to the competencies being evaluated. TPQ uses an adaptive approach in which questions can adjust based on previous responses to explore relevant behavioral areas further. The resulting profile is interpreted against the configured requirements of the role.

The output is a role-configured competency profile. It sets out where a candidate's stated preferences match what the role needs, where there may be gaps, and which areas a hiring manager should explore further in conversation with the candidate.

The report can help hiring managers identify areas for follow-up. In a 2022 re-analysis, Paul Sackett, Charlene Zhang, Christopher Berry and Filip Lievens revised earlier estimates of how well selection methods predict job performance, with structured interviews emerging as the highest-ranked procedure examined. That finding does not validate TPQ's interview prompts. Structured interviews require standardized questions and consistent scoring criteria; TPQ's prompts provide additional areas to explore.

ACHNET is explicit about how far the questionnaire's findings should be taken.

"TPQ supports human judgment. It should not be presented as a pass/fail test, a fixed personality label, or a definitive predictor of job performance," Gupta said.

The company presents the report as material for a conversation. The same findings can carry past the hiring decision, into onboarding priorities and development discussions once the candidate has joined.

TPQ is one stage in ACHNET's platform, alongside applicant ranking, technical assessments, AI video interviews conducted by iJupiter™ and fraud detection. Each produces a different kind of evidence. A resume records experience and qualifications. A technical assessment provides evidence of a candidate's knowledge or skills in the areas assessed. TPQ adds a structured account of how the candidate prefers to work, interpreted against the demands of the specific role.

Holding those inputs in one place lets a hiring team weigh them together when it reaches a decision. Reviewing these inputs together gives hiring teams a broader view of the candidate's experience, demonstrated skills, and workplace behavioral preferences. TPQ contributes one source of evidence alongside assessments, interviews, and other role-relevant information.

TPQ asks about the competencies a specific job needs, makes candidates choose between their own preferences, and passes what it finds to the person running the interview. How much it improves a hire will depend on what that person does with the report, and ACHNET has left that decision with the hiring team.

#9752. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9751. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9750. Alexey Gubarev: Why Investors Are Finally Taking Women's Health Seriously

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

The Business Research Company reports that the global femtech market was worth about $46.5 billion in 2025 and could reach nearly $119 billion by 2030, with an annual growth rate of 20.8%. So, how did femtech move from a niche category to a major investment opportunity, and why are investors now taking women's health seriously? Alexey Gubarev, a tech entrepreneur based in Cyprus, offers his view.

He co-founded Palta, the venture company behind Flo Health, which became the first women’s health app valued at over $1 billion in 2024. He also built Servers.com, a global infrastructure company he led for 18 years before it was sold for $200 million in 2023.

For many years, women's health was seen as a small part of healthcare. Topics like menstruation, fertility, and pregnancy were viewed as specialist areas instead of being recognized as the basis for a much larger healthcare market. Because of this, technology investors often provided limited funding, set cautious valuations, and believed that women's health products had limited growth potential.

That perception is finally beginning to change.

It's not just that women's health is now a more visible social issue. Investors are beginning to see how big the unmet need is, how large the potential market could be, and the chance to build lasting global businesses around problems that have been overlooked for generations.

After years of building technology companies and investing in digital health, I see femtech as one of the most exciting opportunities where technology, healthcare, and consumer behavior meet.

The women's health gap is not a new problem. Research by the McKinsey Health Institute, published in collaboration with the World Economic Forum in 2024, found that women spend approximately 25% more of their lives in poor health than men. The report estimated that addressing this gap could add up to $1 trillion to the global economy annually by 2040.

In the past, medical research and healthcare systems often did not fully consider women's specific needs. Because of this, many conditions were under-researched, underdiagnosed, or not properly addressed. Women have frequently faced complex health questions without reliable, personalized information.

When we established Palta in 2016, our ambition was to empower billions of health-conscious people to live healthier and happier lives. Women's health quickly emerged as one of the clearest opportunities to make a meaningful difference. I talked about the early years at Palta and the apps we started with in this interview with CBN.

About half of the world's population experiences menstruation, but for years there was no credible, technology-based product to address this need on a global scale. We noticed a huge gap between the size of the problem and the solutions that existed.

For investors, this gap should have been a clear sign. Instead, the sector was often seen as niche and overlooked.

In recent years, more digital products have been created to meet women's health needs. What started as a small category focused on period-tracking apps has grown into a much wider range of platforms that cover fertility, pregnancy, hormonal conditions, menopause, and access to specialized medical care.

Several companies illustrate how diverse this market has become.

For example, Maven Clinic has created a virtual healthcare platform that covers fertility, family planning, pregnancy, parenting, and menopause. In October 2024, the company raised $125 million in a Series F round, reaching a reported valuation of $1.7 billion and bringing its total funding to over $425 million. The platform partners with employers and health plans, showing that women's health solutions can also become strong business-to-business healthcare models.

Another example is Midi Health, which focuses on perimenopause, menopause, and midlife women's health. In February 2026, it raised $100 million in Series D funding at a valuation of over $1 billion. This is notable because it shows that investment in women's health is growing beyond fertility and reproductive care into areas that have often been overlooked.

At Palta, we think the best businesses in this field bring together three things: technology that can grow, strong medical expertise, and careful financial management.

The success of Flo and other femtech companies is a big milestone, but it's not the end of the industry's story. It shows what can happen when long-ignored healthcare needs are met with the right mix of technology, science, and good business practices.

We are moving toward a future where a smartphone can act as a personal health companion. It can help women understand their bodies, notice changes, find reliable information, and have better conversations with healthcare professionals throughout their lives.

Advanced AI, medical research, and more sophisticated digital platforms will speed up this change. But technology by itself won't close the women's health gap. That will take ongoing investment in research, stronger clinical evidence, better access to healthcare, and products built around what women really need.

For investors, the question is no longer whether women's health is a real market. The rising number of femtech companies, their growing user bases, and the investments they attract show that this is a business category that matters more and more.

The bigger question is how many other major healthcare opportunities are still undiscovered simply because we haven't been paying enough attention.

A co-founder of Servers.com, Palta and TechIsland, Alexey Gubarev is based in Limassol, Cyprus. Alongside his work as an entrepreneur and investor, he is a collector whose retro car museum is expected to open at Bishkek’s former Western Bus Station in 2027. #9749. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.
