Posted on Nov 16 • Originally published at Medium

Token, sandbox, POST /api/pix/cashIn, tratamento do webhook e confirmação de status, com exemplos em curl e PHP/Laravel

Sou diretor de projetos da PushinPay. Boa parte do meu dia é ajudar times a ligar o Pix no sistema deles: loja virtual, plataforma de infoproduto, ERP. As dúvidas se repetem: onde pego o token, como gero o QR Code, como sei que o cliente pagou, o que faço quando o webhook chega duas vezes.

Este texto junta o que a gente costuma explicar nessas conversas. São exemplos em curl, para testar no terminal, e em PHP com Laravel, para colar no projeto.

Mande também Accept: application/json em todas as chamadas. Assim a resposta, inclusive a de erro, vem sempre em JSON.

Uma dica de organização: guarde a URL base e o token em variáveis de ambiente. Trocar de sandbox para produção vira só mudar o .env.

A cobrança é criada com POST /api/pix/cashIn. O único campo de que você realmente precisa é value, em centavos. O mínimo é 50, ou seja, R$ 0,50.

Os outros campos são opcionais, mas na prática eu uso quase todos:

Em curl, uma cobrança de R$ 49,90 com validade de 30 minutos fica assim:

A resposta traz o que você precisa para mostrar ao cliente:

Repare no ?pedido=1234 na webhook_url. É um truque simples: quando o aviso chegar, você já sabe de qual pedido se trata, sem depender de nada do corpo da requisição.

No Laravel, o cliente HTTP nativo resolve. Primeiro, coloque as variáveis em config/services.php:

Depois, no ponto em que o pedido é fechado:

Na view, o QR Code aparece direto do base64. Se o campo já vier com o prefixo data:image/png;base64,, use como está; se não vier, acrescente o prefixo:

Deixe sempre o copia e cola visível ao lado da imagem. Quem está comprando pelo celular não consegue escanear a própria tela.

Toda a lógica do pedido gira em torno de quatro valores de status:

O mapeamento para o seu sistema costuma ser direto: paid libera o pedido, canceled devolve o estoque, refunded dispara o fluxo de devolução.

Quando o status muda, a PushinPay faz um POST na webhook_url. Se preferir não mandar a URL em cada cobrança, dá para configurar um webhook por conta em /api/accounts/webhooks.

Se você configurar um segredo, as requisições chegam com dois headers: x-pushinpay-token e x-pushinpay-signature, no formato sha256=. Valide antes de processar qualquer coisa. Os detalhes de como montar a comparação estão na documentação.

A regra que eu repito em toda integração: não trate o webhook como a verdade final. Use o aviso como gatilho e confirme o status consultando a transação. Isso é boa prática para qualquer gateway, não algo específico nosso.

Lembre de tirar essa rota da verificação de CSRF. E o controller:

Três detalhes nesse código fazem diferença em produção:

Se o seu servidor ficar fora do ar e algum webhook falhar, dá para reenviar pelo painel ou pela API.

Além da consulta que já apareceu no webhook, mais dois endpoints entram cedo na integração:

Vale ter também uma rotina agendada que consulta pedidos parados em created há mais tempo que o expires_in. É uma rede de segurança barata para o caso raro de um aviso se perder no caminho.

Se a sua aplicação também precisa pagar alguém (repasse a afiliado, devolução manual), o saque usa POST /api/pix/cashOut com value em centavos (mínimo 100, R$ 1,00), pix_key, receiver_national_registration e webhook_url. A consulta fica em GET /api/transfers/{id}.

Aqui tem um ponto de segurança: o token precisa de permissão de transferência. Eu recomendo usar um token separado para saque, guardado só no serviço que faz isso, e não o mesmo do checkout.

Se travar em algum ponto, o time da PushinPay acompanha a integração sem custo, e na maioria dos casos ela fica pronta em menos de 12 horas.

#9734. Engineering Zero-State Search

I am an Engineering leader with over 15+ years experience building multi billion user, large scale, low latency and ML driven monetization

I am an Engineering leader with over 15+ years experience building multi billion user, large scale, low latency and ML driven monetization

I am an Engineering leader with over 15+ years experience building multi billion user, large scale, low latency and ML driven monetization

Open Spotify, Netflix, or almost any modern delivery app, and tap the search bar. Before you type a single letter, the screen is already full. You see recent genres, trending queries, categories tailored to the time of day, or items you lingered on yesterday.

In information retrieval, this is the zero-state search.

Traditional search engines are reactive. They wait for a text string, parse tokens, hit an inverted index or vector store, and rank candidates against explicit intent. zero-state search flips that sequence. The ranking decision happens before the user expresses any intent at all.

That shift sounds like a minor UI convenience, but it changes the underlying systems problem. When you populate a search screen ahead of the first keystroke, you are trading explicit intent for latency and convenience. Get it right, and the user saves five seconds of typing. Get it wrong, and you have built a high-speed wall of stale, repetitive guesses that gets in the way of actual search.

Here is how the engineering problem changes when ranking moves ahead of the query—and why standard offline relevance metrics usually fail to catch the worst UX bugs.

When a user taps into a search bar, your latency budget is unforgiving. If  zero-state suggestions take 400ms to pop in, the user has already started typing, and the UI jump when the suggestions finally render will cause mis-taps. To feel native, zero-state payloads need to resolve in under 50ms to 100ms—often served straight from a local device cache or an edge key-value store.

Because you cannot run heavy multi-stage ranking at tap time, the work moves earlier. Candidate generation and scoring happen asynchronously: in nightly batch jobs, on app launch, or triggered by background event streams.

Precomputation buys you speed, but it creates an immediate freshness problem.

Suppose a user spends twenty minutes browsing hiking boots on an e-commerce app, buys a pair, and closes the app. If your  zero-state pipeline relies on a batch job that recomputes user embeddings every six hours, the next time that user taps the search bar, your system will proudly suggest hiking boots. The prediction had a high offline probability score, but in the real world, the task is over.

To make precomputed rankings work without feeling broken, teams usually have to split the scoring pipeline into two layers:

The Slow Layer (Batch/Nearline): Computes broad affinity scores, collaborative filtering candidates, and long-term category preferences. This populates the candidate pool.

The Fast Re-ranker (Edge/Client-side): Applies lightweight, deterministic rules at read time. It checks local session state, filters out items purchased or dismissed in the last ten minutes, and adjusts weights based on immediate context (like time of day or device connection).

If you only build the slow layer, your app will feel like it has amnesia about what the user just did.

The most common mistake in  zero-state ranking is reusing the exact same objective function used for standard search or home-feed click-through rate (CTR).

When a user types "wireless mechanical keyboard", narrowing the results to ten nearly identical keyboards is a win. You have an explicit constraint. Before a query, you have no constraint. If your model notices a user clicked on Italian restaurants twice last week and responds by filling every slot on the  zero-state screen with pasta places, you haven't built a discovery tool. You've built a rut.

High pointwise scores do not equal a useful screen. If five candidates each have a 15% probability of being clicked, but all five represent the exact same intent cluster, showing all five wastes four slots.

Instead of pure relevance sorting, zero-state ranking has to be treated as a portfolio optimization problem (or a slated recommendation problem). The goal isn't for every item on the screen to be right; the goal is for at least one item on the screen to match the user's unspoken mood.

In practice, this requires a few structural guardrails in the ranking logic:

Intent Clustering & Deduplication: Group candidates by semantic category or task before final slot allocation. Cap how many slots any single cluster can claim, regardless of raw model score.

Impression Decay (Fatigue Penalties): If a user has seen a  zero-state suggestion three times across three sessions and ignored it every time, its score should decay aggressively. Without impression discounting, static high-prior items (like a user's all-time top genre) will squat on the top slot forever.

Dedicated Exploration Slots: Reserve 10% to 20% of the visible real estate for low-confidence, high-variance candidates or trending global queries. If you never show anything outside the user's historical profile, the model can only reinforce its own past predictions.

Every proactive recommendation carries an implicit risk: it is a guess made on the user's behalf, and most of the time, guesses miss.

When a recommendation misses on a passive browse feed, the cost is low—the user just keeps scrolling. When a recommendation misses on a search screen, the user is often trying to accomplish a specific task. If your  zero-state interface hijacks the screen, pushes the keyboard down, or requires an extra tap to clear a pre-filled suggestion, a wrong guess actively slows the user down.

Good  zero-state systems are designed to be ignored at zero cost.

That means the boundary between "browsing suggestions" and "typing a query" has to be frictionless. The text cursor should be focused and ready. The moment the first character is typed, the  zero-state state should yield immediately to prefix autocomplete without layout lag. Users shouldn't have to fight the system's prediction to state their actual intent.

How do you know if your  zero-state ranking is actually helping users, rather than just farming accidental taps?

Looking at the click-through rate on the  zero-state screen in isolation is a trap. You can easily inflate zero-state CTR by making the suggestion cards huge, hiding the keyboard by default, or showing clickbait trending topics. Your  zero-state metrics will go up while overall search satisfaction tanks.

Engineers working on pre-query systems should evaluate the entire session trajectory, not just the first tap:

Downstream Task Completion (Assisted Success): When a user clicks a  zero-state suggestion, do they actually complete a downstream action (play a song, read an article, add to cart), or do they immediately bounce back to the search bar and type a manual query? A click followed by an immediate back-navigation within 3 seconds is a false positive.

Time-to-Success: Compare sessions that start with a  zero-state tap against sessions that start with manual typing. Does the precomputed screen actually reduce the time it takes for a user to find something they engage with?

Query Reformulation & Abandonment Rate: If introducing a new  zero-state ranking model increases the rate at which users abandon the search tab entirely, your suggestions are likely creating visual noise or decision fatigue.

Slot Entropy / Refresh Rate: Measure how often the top N slots actually change for a given user across consecutive sessions. If your jaccard similarity between Tuesday's screen and Wednesday's screen is 0.95, your freshness signals are under-weighted.

Moving ranking ahead of the first keystroke doesn't replace search. Plenty of users open an app knowing the exact string they want to type, and the best thing a system can do for them is stay out of the way.

But for the users who open search with a half-formed goal—looking for something to watch, something to eat, or a topic they were researching yesterday—the  zero-state screen is where retrieval actually begins. Treating that screen as a first-class systems problem means looking past raw prediction scores. It requires balancing precomputed speed with real-time session context, penalizing repetition, and designing an interface that lets the user overrule the algorithm without missing a beat.

The Millisecond Conundrum: Balancing Latency, Freshness, and Intelligence at Scale

#9733. How We Built a Remote 10-Tool Streamable HTTP MCP Server and 13.3 KiB Link-in-Bio in Go

Public link-in-bio pages are structurally simple documents: an avatar, a name, a contact bar, and 5 to 20 links. Yet most commercial bio-link platforms render them as client-heavy Single-Page Applications that download hundreds of kilobytes of framework JavaScript inside Instagram, TikTok, or WhatsApp in-app WebViews before painting a button.

When we built Linq.es and its Official Remote MCP Server (https://linq.es/mcp), we took the opposite path on both the public frontend and the AI agent layer:

Below are the main architectural lessons we learned building both layers in Go.

Most link-in-bio clicks happen inside constrained mobile WebViews (Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, and WhatsApp) over variable cellular connections. Every extra script tag, font round-trip, and client hydration pass delays First Contentful Paint and increases bounce rates before a visitor taps a wa.me button or downloads a .vcf contact card.

On Linq.es, public profiles render complete semantic HTML in the European Union behind a multi-tier cache (in-memory L1, persistent object storage L2, and Cloudflare Edge CDN):

No third-party ad pixels (Meta, TikTok, or GA4) are injected on public pages unless a Pro profile owner explicitly configures their own measurement IDs.

Many early MCP integrations wrap an existing REST API inside a local Node.js stdio package that users run via npx -y @vendor/mcp-server. That introduces three recurring friction points:

With the 2025-03-26 Streamable HTTP specification, an MCP server runs as a standard HTTPS JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint:

During the MCP handshake, right after initialize succeeds, strict clients send a JSON-RPC notification ({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}) that omits the id field. If your HTTP router wraps every return path in a 200 OK JSON-RPC envelope with "id": null, strict clients treat the unexpected body as a protocol error.

In Go + Gin, handling JSON-RPC notifications before dispatching methods keeps the handshake clean:

On serverless container platforms, CPU allocation drops as soon as the HTTP response finishes writing. If an AI agent calls add_profile_link or update_profile_link and you trigger CDN cache purges in detached background goroutines, the container can be throttled before the outbound purge completes, leaving visitors looking at stale HTML when the agent reports the link is live.

Running storage and CDN cache invalidations concurrently inside a sync.WaitGroup before returning the tools/call response guarantees that by the time Claude or Cursor replies "Done, live at https://linq.es/handle", public visitors already see the updated page:

When exposing read, write, and delete operations side by side, tool descriptions alone should not force an LLM host to guess which calls are safe to auto-approve and which require human confirmation.

Adding standard MCP annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint) using explicit boolean pointers in Go ensures false values serialize cleanly instead of being dropped by omitempty:

Combined with "additionalProperties": false on every tool's inputSchema and clear prerequisite notes (e.g., calling list_profiles to discover handles and list_profile_links before update_profile_link or delete_profile_link), agents avoid hallucinating parameters or accidentally deleting links when a user only asked to hide one (active: false).

Once you generate a Personal API Key in Account Settings, you can connect Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json), Claude Desktop, Windsurf, or Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json) directly over HTTPS:

From there, your agent can use all 10 tools across up to 5 profiles and 500 /s/ shortlinks:

You can inspect the live discovery metadata anytime with curl -s https://linq.es/mcp | jq ., try the free .vcf, WhatsApp, and UTM generators without an account at https://linq.es/tools, or read the full MCP setup docs at https://linq.es/integrations/mcp.

#9731. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

Explore live Granite LLMON instruction attention

That's really awesome! With an Apple pkl community renderer, you could potentially write PKL and render LLMON. 🥒🍋

Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

#9730. Exposing ThingsDB as a MySQL Database

Integrating a high-speed, object-oriented database with traditional reporting tools, BI dashboards, or legacy applications often hits a familiar roadblock: most external tools expect SQL.

With the new MySQL Endpoint module (module-go-mysqlendpoint), ThingsDB can now speak the MySQL wire protocol directly. This allows you to connect standard MySQL clients, BI tools (like Grafana, Metabase, or Power BI), and existing SQL drivers straight to your ThingsDB collections, no ETL pipelines or data duplication required.

Because ThingsDB modules run across every node in your cluster, the MySQL endpoint is automatically available on all ThingsDB nodes. Since every node reads directly from the synchronized cluster state, you get built-in high availability and load-balancing capabilities for your SQL connections right out of the box.

Installing and configuring the module takes just a few lines in the @thingsdb scope:

By default, the module listens on port 3306 and automatically creates a dedicated schema collection (configurable via schema_scope) where you define your virtual MySQL database, tables, columns, and users.

Rather than forcing your ThingsDB data into rigid SQL tables on disk, the module lets you map ThingsDB queries to virtual MySQL tables:

Whenever you update your virtual schema in the schema collection, simply call mysqlendpoint.reload() to apply the changes without restarting your nodes. You can find a complete example in the repository.

One of the biggest advantages of exposing ThingsDB via virtual queries is how cleanly you can handle multi-tenancy and per-user data isolation within a single database:

Whether you want to plug a BI dashboard into live cluster metrics or give external services read access to isolated tenant collections, the MySQL Endpoint module bridges the gap with minimal setup.

Check out the full documentation, configuration options, and a complete runnable example in the module-go-mysqlendpoint repository.

#9728. NEXORA — Beyond the Frame: a cinematic skin for Video.js v10

I built NEXORA — Beyond the Frame, a cinematic dark-glass skin for Video.js v10, and entered it in the Video.js Skins Design Challenge by Mux.

NEXORA is built on the real Video.js v10 HTML renderer (@videojs/html) with the Mux video component (@videojs/mux-video). The demo runs against a Mux-hosted video with chapters and English/Japanese subtitle tracks. The skin passed an axe-core accessibility audit with zero violations, and every control is a real Video.js component — nothing is a painted mockup.

The project is open source under the Apache-2.0 license, with architecture, customization and accessibility documentation in the repo.

Feedback from video and frontend folks is very welcome — especially on the accessibility pass and the timeline previews.

#9727. Beyond Green CI: Building a More Trustworthy DevSecOps Pipeline

How real container images, security checks, and CI failures helped improve the InfraPulse security pipeline.

In Part 1 — 12 Green CI Jobs, 422 Security Findings, I shared an important lesson: even when all required CI checks pass, security scanners can still report hundreds of findings that need further investigation.

In Part 2 — From 422 Security Findings to Auditable Evidence, I explored how InfraPulse evolved to produce more reliable evidence about software components, artifact integrity, and the software supply chain.

How can we make sure these security checks still work when we move beyond controlled tests and start analyzing real container images?

That became the focus of the next stage of InfraPulse, an open-source monitoring and observability platform I am building to explore software engineering, DevOps, DevSecOps, and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) through practical implementation.

The goal was to improve the security pipeline by connecting previously verified evidence to real container image analysis.

This article covers what changed, the challenges I encountered, and the lessons learned along the way.

Imagine an application running inside a Docker container.

That container includes the application itself, operating system files, libraries, and other dependencies required to run.

Before using the image, we might want to answer a few questions:

These questions sound similar, but they address different concerns.

For example, a valid digital signature can help verify that an artifact has not changed and that it was signed using a key accepted by a configured trust policy.

However, it does not automatically prove that every dependency was discovered or establish the real-world identity of the person or system that built the image.

Similarly, two inventories may match without either one containing every component.

The first important lesson was that successful verification must come with clearly defined limits.

InfraPulse already had mechanisms for validating security evidence, including digital signatures, artifact information, and software component inventories.

One of these inventories is called an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials).

Think of an SBOM as an ingredient list for software. It records known components and dependencies associated with an application.

The next step was to compare this information with the contents of real container images using the OCI format, a standard widely used in the container ecosystem.

Before exploring the implementation details, it helps to understand how the different security checks fit together.

The following diagram provides a high-level overview of the InfraPulse security pipeline, from source code and CI checks to container analysis, evidence verification, and reporting.

Figure 1 — InfraPulse Security Pipeline Overview. Conceptual overview of code quality checks, container image analysis, security evidence, signature verification, and OCI inventory reconciliation. The pipeline preserves explicit coverage limitations rather than treating successful CI execution as proof of complete security.

The diagram highlights an important idea: security is not a single check performed at the end of development.

It involves multiple activities, including code quality, testing, vulnerability analysis, artifact integrity, and evidence verification.

Each activity contributes useful information, but no individual check can guarantee that an application is completely secure.

The integration implemented in this stage follows five main steps:

Imagine a system verifies a file and then opens the same file path again a few seconds later.

If the file changes between those operations, the system might end up processing something different from what it originally verified.

To avoid that inconsistency, InfraPulse passes forward the exact data snapshot that was verified.

Verifying an artifact is not enough. We also need to ensure that the data we use afterward is the data that passed verification.

This integration was delivered through Pull Request #15.

The post-merge GitHub Actions workflow completed successfully.

The implementation reuses the existing signed-evidence verifier instead of introducing a separate signature-verification mechanism.

This reduces duplicated logic and helps maintain consistent verification behavior.

However, the historical signing materials used in an earlier execution were not preserved with the real-image artifacts.

As a result, that exact historical signed execution cannot be reproduced.

The integration was exercised through automated tests, including mocked verifier interactions and real Cosign signing and verification in CI using disposable keys.

These tests provide evidence that the implemented components work under the tested conditions.

They do not reproduce the original historical signature chain.

This distinction matters because testing an integration and reproducing a specific historical verification are not the same thing.

During development, small and controlled test files are extremely useful.

They make it easier to reproduce specific situations, such as invalid paths, malformed archives, or unexpected file structures.

But real container images are more complicated.

In this stage of the project, I worked with preserved archives from two images:

These images contained variations of TAR archive metadata that the earlier tests did not fully represent.

The image layer reader had to be extended to support the observed formats, including USTAR, a GNU TAR header variant, and selected PAX metadata.

A container image is not just one compressed file.

It contains layers that describe changes to a filesystem. Understanding the resulting content requires interpreting those layers and their metadata correctly.

If a tool encounters an unfamiliar format, guessing how to interpret it can produce misleading results.

For this reason, the implementation follows a simple rule:

If the reader encounters an unsupported structure, it rejects the input instead of silently accepting it.

It does not make the reader compatible with every possible container image format. Instead, it helps prevent unsupported data from being treated as successfully analyzed.

Some valid archive variations, such as compressed layers or unsupported PAX extensions, may still require additional implementation work.

The validation used image archives preserved from an earlier GitHub Actions execution.

In total, 24 layers were processed, with checks against recorded file hashes, image identifiers, and layer information.

These figures come from the project's validation report and should be confirmed against the retained execution evidence before publication.

The result demonstrated that the reader could process those specific real images and their observed archive formats.

It did not prove universal OCI compatibility or complete detection of every software component.

Figure 2 — Real OCI Image Validation. InfraPulse analyzed two preserved container images: Backend and Nginx. Each image contained 12 processed layers, generating a total of 13,309 inventory entries and 10,492 files with content hashes. The validation included image identity and integrity checks, along with inventory comparison against the verified SBOM. The reported status remained COVERAGE_PARTIAL, indicating that successful validation does not guarantee universal OCI compatibility or complete identification of all software components.

Another important lesson was that security tools need protection too.

Imagine receiving an unexpectedly large archive or one containing an excessive number of filesystem entries.

Even without malicious code, processing that archive could consume too much memory, overload the CPU, or interrupt a service.

To reduce that risk, I introduced explicit limits into the OCI layer reader.

Additional restrictions cover file path length and depth.

These values are specific defensive choices made for this implementation, not universal requirements of the OCI specification.

These controls protect the reader, but they do not automatically protect every step before it.

For example, a downloader could load an oversized archive into memory before the reader has an opportunity to reject it.

A production-oriented solution therefore needs resource controls throughout the process, including:

This is an example of defense in depth: using multiple layers of protection rather than relying on a single security check.

The same principle applies to other systems that process external files, including backup tools, document processors, and software deployment pipelines.

During the implementation, GitHub Actions detected a Python formatting issue.

The check was performed by Ruff, a tool used to enforce code quality and formatting rules.

This was not a security vulnerability or a major architectural problem. The code simply did not meet one of the project's established quality requirements.

After correcting the formatting issue, the required checks were executed again and passed.

The workflow after the pull request was merged also completed successfully.

The goal of CI is not to stay green at all costs. Its purpose is to catch problems before they become part of the codebase.

A failure that is detected, understood, and corrected shows that a quality control is doing its job.

The same reasoning applies to security checks.

We need to distinguish between situations such as:

Treating them as equivalent can create a false sense of security.

Figure 3 — GitHub Actions Validation. The initial Ruff formatting failure was corrected before merge, followed by successful required checks and a successful post-merge workflow. Passing CI does not establish that the application is free from vulnerabilities.

By the end of this implementation stage, InfraPulse could validate the expected image information, process the supported layers, and compare image inventories against previously verified data.

Even so, the final result retained an explicit status:

Why keep that status after so many checks succeeded?

Because three concepts need to remain separate.

Integrity: Does the data match the expected values?

Authenticity: What can we establish about the identity or authority behind an artifact or signature?

Completeness: Have all relevant software components actually been identified?

A tool may successfully verify file integrity without proving who originally built the image.

Likewise, it may compare two inventories without proving that either inventory is complete.

That is why InfraPulse does not turn a successful comparison into a claim of complete software coverage.

The project also does not claim to have achieved a particular SLSA level.

The 422 records were scanner-reported occurrences across different tools and targets. They were not necessarily 422 unique, confirmed, exploitable vulnerabilities.

This stage of the project did not demonstrate that all those findings had been eliminated.

A green CI pipeline does not mean zero vulnerabilities. It means the configured required checks passed under the conditions they evaluated.

Understanding that distinction is essential when interpreting security results.

It also explains why maintaining the COVERAGE_PARTIAL status is useful.

Instead of presenting a stronger guarantee than the available evidence supports, the pipeline makes its coverage limitations explicit.

This stage of InfraPulse brought several lessons that apply beyond this particular project.

When an artifact passes validation, avoid later using another version that could have changed.

This applies to SBOMs, configuration files, deployment manifests, and other security-sensitive data.

Trusted keys, expected image identifiers, and verification policies should not be defined solely by the artifact being examined.

Otherwise, an artifact could effectively set its own acceptance rules.

Small test fixtures help reproduce specific problems.

Real artifacts reveal compatibility issues and unexpected details that controlled tests may miss.

Both approaches are valuable, but they answer different questions.

A parser limit cannot prevent excessive memory usage if the downloader has already loaded a huge file.

Resource controls need to cover every relevant stage.

A valid signature, a matching inventory, a successful scanner execution, and a green CI result are all useful.

Reliable engineering means understanding what each result confirms—and what remains uncertain.

That was probably the most valuable lesson from this implementation.

The planned integration was completed, but several opportunities for improvement remain.

One is extending image format compatibility while maintaining safe parsing behavior.

Another is improving the ability to reproduce earlier security validations.

Different categories of evidence currently have different retention periods:

This means a report may remain available after the original files needed to reproduce its results have already been removed.

Additionally, the disposable signing materials used in an earlier historical verification were not preserved, so that exact signed execution cannot be replayed.

This revealed another important distinction:

Keeping a report is not necessarily the same as preserving everything required to reproduce it.

Evidence retention and reproducibility are related, but they are not identical.

A project may retain summary reports for weeks while no longer having access to the exact image archives or signatures used in an earlier verification.

This is something worth considering when designing CI/CD pipelines that need to support audits or repeatable investigations.

Beyond the security pipeline, future areas of exploration include service-level indicators, actionable alerts, failure recovery, and repeatable operational procedures.

These are potential improvements, not features being claimed as completed here.

Figure 4 — Evidence Retention and Reproducibility. Image archives, sanitized reports, and unsigned CI evidence have different retention periods. Preserving a report does not necessarily preserve all materials required to reproduce the original verification.

This stage of InfraPulse demonstrated that implementing security controls is only part of the challenge.

We also need to verify that those controls work with real files, handle unexpected inputs safely, and produce results that can be interpreted correctly.

But the most important lesson was understanding that a reliable system must recognize its own limits.

A green pipeline, a valid signature, or a well-structured report is not enough on its own.

We need to understand what each result actually proves.

InfraPulse continues to evolve as an open-source project focused on practical software engineering, DevOps, DevSecOps, and SRE.

GitHub: https://github.com/jacivaldocarvalho/jc-infrapulse

There are still challenges to explore, solutions to test, and lessons to share.

#9726. How Foreign Businesses Can Accept UPI Payments and Subscriptions in India

India has one of the world’s largest digital audiences - and a payment environment that can punish assumptions imported from the United States or Europe. A checkout that supports international cards may technically accept a payment from India, but that does not mean it fits how a typical Indian customer prefers to pay. The opportunity is not simply to display prices in rupees. It is to choose the right rail, authorization experience, commercial partner, and renewal architecture.

UPI deserves to be treated as a first-class option, not because cards are irrelevant, but because a card-only strategy can unnecessarily limit reach. Equally important: accepting a one-time UPI payment is not the same as making recurring UPI billing work for a foreign merchant. The distinction is where a large part of the engineering effort begins.

India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) handled 241.62 billion transactions worth approximately ₹314.23 lakh crore in FY2025-26, according to a government release drawing on NPCI data. The number of transactions was around five times the FY2021-22 level. By June 2026, roughly 554.9 million users had been onboarded to UPI.

These figures tell us that UPI has achieved extraordinary breadth; they do not, by themselves, prove its conversion rate for an online subscription checkout. UPI transaction totals span different use cases, including transfers between individuals and payments to merchants. Comparing every UPI transaction with only credit-card purchase transactions would be an apples-to-oranges comparison. The relevant question for a seller is narrower: how much of its own target audience can pay successfully, and how readily, with each method?

That distinction matters. A foreign business does not need to replace cards completely. It should test whether adding UPI to a well-designed checkout increases payment completion among its intended Indian customers, without compromising subscription operations or compliance.

A credit card is a convenient default for many American subscription products. In India, it is a less universal starting point. Credit cards depend on issuer underwriting and access to a line of credit. RBI directions require issuers to assess an applicant's credit risk with reference to their independent financial means. Cards in circulation are also not the same as distinct people who hold an active, usable card.

The problem is both availability and checkout readiness. RBI card-security rules require cards to be issued with domestic ATM and point-of-sale use enabled as the baseline, while cardholders can control online and international transaction settings. An Indian customer may have a card yet be unable to complete a cross-border, card-not-present transaction until they change issuer settings. That failure can look like an ordinary declined payment to the merchant.

Preference also matters, but it deserves more careful language than a national stereotype. UPI’s familiarity, immediate account-based payment experience, wide merchant acceptance, and lack of a revolving credit requirement can make it appealing to customers who have access to both methods. Rather than assume all Indian consumers dislike credit, businesses should measure customer preferences, available instruments, authorization success and payment-method selection in their own funnel.

The market is connected, but willingness to pay varies widely. TRAI reports approximately 1.09 billion internet subscriptions as of March 2026. The FICCI-EY analysis estimates that Indian digital-subscription revenue grew 60% to ₹163 billion in calendar 2025, including video, audio and news. Within video, its estimates show 216 million paid subscriptions across 143 million households, many accessed through bundled offers.

These numbers demonstrate growth and market diversity; they should not be used to infer that the average paid video subscription costs ₹63 a month. The ₹163 billion revenue total covers more than video, the 216 million count refers to video subscriptions, and bundles complicate the relationship between subscriptions and what end users pay directly. A headline blended “price” created by dividing those incompatible figures would be misleading.

For a foreign merchant, pricing solely in dollars may mean a foreign-currency card purchase, possible issuer conversion fees, and a price on the statement that differs from the amount shown at checkout. The exact cost depends on the card, issuer and transaction arrangement. Card restrictions can also affect payment success. INR pricing paired with a viable local collection flow can reduce those sources of customer friction, but the business still needs to account for local taxes, foreign exchange and settlement costs within its own economics.

The practical takeaway: build the Indian price from customer value, competition, tax treatment, and payment economics. Do not calculate it solely by multiplying a US list price by the spot exchange rate.

UPI is an interoperable, real-time payment system operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). A customer typically initiates or approves a payment in a UPI-enabled app linked to their bank account. The merchant and its payment partners receive a transaction result, while bank-account identifiers need not be entered on the merchant’s checkout page. It is more accurate to say the account credential is not exposed to the merchant than to say no credential or identifying information ever travels through the payment network.

A merchant can present an app-intent link on mobile or a QR-based flow on desktop; a collect flow may also be supported depending on the provider and use case. Availability, customer prompts, and conversion vary by product and UPI app. The only reliable way to pick the checkout UX is to test the actual payment paths, including app switches, slow callbacks, user cancellations and return-to-merchant behavior.

Historically, bank-account-funded UPI merchant transactions operated largely under a zero-MDR framework. A September 2026 announcement set out a 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) for eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more. Person-to-person transfers, payments of ₹2,000 or less, and qualifying small-merchant transactions remain exempt; some sectors have lower or flat rates.

For subscription businesses, one-time checkout and recurring collection need to be distinguished. NPCI’s policy FAQ expressly states that automated recurring standing instructions (UPI AutoPay mandates), including OTT subscriptions, do not attract the prescribed MDR. This exemption concerns the network MDR; it should not be mistaken for a guarantee that gateways, aggregators, or cross-border providers will charge no processing, settlement, or foreign-exchange fees.

The announced rates were initially scheduled for October 15, 2026, but NPCI deferred the rollout until after Diwali. As of November 13, 2026, no replacement effective date had been confirmed. MDR is a merchant-acceptance cost, not an extra UPI checkout surcharge to the customer. Merchants should confirm the effective date, applicable transaction classifications including mandate renewals and their actual provider fee schedule and net settlement with the acquiring or aggregation partner. Broad claims that UPI is always free for merchants, or that the new 0.4% MDR already applies to all UPI payments, are misleading.

For subscriptions, UPI AutoPay adds an electronic mandate. The customer authorizes its setup, and later debit attempts are made against that mandate subject to network, bank, regulatory and mandate-specific rules. The payment provider - not the merchant alone implements the network interactions; the merchant must still maintain the correct business state.

Under RBI’s Digital Payments – E-mandate Framework, 2026, recurring transactions up to ₹15,000 generally may proceed without additional authentication after mandate setup; higher authentication-free thresholds apply to specified categories such as insurance, mutual funds and credit-card bills. Issuers generally must send a pre-debit notification at least 24 hours before charging, subject to stated exceptions. This requires advance scheduling and coordination; it does not mean that every same-day debit is prohibited or that a merchant should blindly charge a day early.

The critical architecture distinction is that subscription state and mandate state are independent. A subscription may remain active in the product database after a customer pauses or revokes the payment mandate in their UPI app. A mandate may be valid when the renewal request is created but fail during execution. Every renewal needs its own attempt, result, retries and reconciliation against the authoritative provider events.

A foreign business has several possible entry models: an Indian entity collecting locally, an arrangement with an Indian payment aggregator and a compliant cross-border settlement path, or a merchant-of-record (MoR) service that contracts with the end customer as seller. These models differ materially in who sells the product, who owns tax and refunds, whose name appears on the customer’s statement, where funds settle, and who handles disputes.

Do not assume that registering a foreign merchant with a globally known processor automatically enables Indian UPI collection. Nor is a locally incorporated subsidiary the only theoretical route. RBI’s Payment Aggregator–Cross Border (PA-CB) framework regulates entities facilitating import and export payments. The actual permissible configuration depends on the authorized entities and their arrangements.

A processor’s brand name is less important than the regulated entity providing the service. Ask the provider for the legal entity name, its relevant RBI authorization, the cross-border direction in which the payment is classified, the bank/settlement chain and the specific supported merchant category. The “inward” and “outward” labels can be confusing if read from the foreign seller’s point of view: check the RBI definitions and the exact transaction flow rather than guessing from a label.

Licensing does not itself establish product availability. A provider may be authorized for cross-border collection yet offer UPI only to certain industries, currencies, checkout integrations or one-time transactions. Ask explicitly whether one-time UPI, mandate registration and renewal debits are enabled for a foreign-registered business in your category. Examples of published provider documentation for cross-border UPI mandates now exist, including PayU’s cross-border UPI consent flow and Paddle’s UPI AutoPay offering; eligibility and contracting still need confirmation.

For recurring billing, obtain the answers before integration: Does the provider offer mandate registration, cancellation, pause, and status queries? Who sends the pre-debit notice? What time windows and retry limits apply? Which transaction results are final, and which are pending? How do asynchronous provider webhooks map to subscription, invoice, and entitlement states? What recovery experience is available after mandate revocation?

Store mandates as separate records linked to subscriptions; make debit and webhook processing idempotent; reconcile transaction IDs with the provider; handle delayed and reversed results; and provide a card or alternative-method recovery path when AutoPay is unavailable. Do not mark an invoice paid merely because the mandate exists or the debit request was accepted.

Digital supplies to Indian consumers may create Indian GST obligations, including under rules for online information and database access or retrieval (OIDAR) services. The responsible party depends on the transaction and seller-of-record structure. Tax obligations do not vanish because the payment uses UPI or because a third party processes funds. Have an India-qualified tax adviser validate the specific service, customer types and contractual arrangements.

Your margin model should separately account for INR list price, applicable tax, provider and settlement fees, currency conversion, chargebacks or disputes where relevant, refunds and payment-recovery expenses. Even with a simple consumer-facing checkout, the underlying economics are not automatically simple.

Consider a digital publisher offering a US subscription at $12 per month. The first launch uses an international-card checkout with dollar pricing. A later, localized experiment offers ₹999 per month, displays the applicable tax treatment clearly, supports eligible local payment methods, and routes UPI through a provider that has confirmed this merchant’s contract and product eligibility.

The ₹999 figure is intentionally illustrative - not a foreign-exchange conversion, market benchmark, or actual business result. The real decision would require price research and controlled testing. The operational differences are more important than the numbers:

USD price; issuer FX may affect statement amount

INR price; taxes and merchant FX/settlement modeled

Cards plus approved UPI flow; app/QR UX tested

Card credential/network token and card rules

UPI AutoPay only where contractually supported; mandate state tracked

Revoked or failed mandates, fallback payments and explicit reauthorization

Checkout starts and accepted card charges

Net paid conversion, first renewal, recovered revenue and support burden

What would prove the strategy works? Not UPI’s national market share. Measure paid checkout conversion by payment method, first-cycle authorization success, the proportion of customers able to register recurring mandates, renewal collection rate after 30 and 60 days, net realized revenue, refund/support cost, and payment-method fallback. Segment those metrics by app, device, acquisition channel, and price cohort.

UPI is not a logo to add next to Visa and Mastercard. It changes the customer’s payment behavior, the merchant’s collection choices and, for recurring revenue, the authorization model itself. But the case for UPI should not be overstated: national transaction totals are not a merchant conversion study, not every foreign seller can activate every UPI product, and fee policy is evolving.

The right approach is to combine local pricing research, a compliant collection chain, carefully tested UPI and card experiences, and an architecture that treats mandates as live customer-controlled permissions. Real localization means adapting the payment architecture to the market - not merely translating the price into its currency.

Author’s note: Sources for the original article were checked on 19 October 2026. Inline source links and the merchant-fee section were reviewed and updated on 13 November 2026. Provider capabilities, fees, and regulations can change; confirm them again before launching. This article is business and engineering analysis, not legal or tax advice.

#9725. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9724. How do you architect robust Playwright E2E tests to validate coordinated UI state consistency across multiple, interconn

Posted on Nov 16 • Originally published at styrow.dev

🔥 Playwright Alert: Is your SPA's UI consistency causing flaky E2E tests?

⚠️ 90% of engineers struggle to reliably validate complex, coordinated UI state across multiple components in Playwright. Here's how to master it.

In sophisticated Single-Page Applications (SPAs), especially dashboards, user actions or backend pushes trigger cascaded, asynchronous UI updates across interconnected components. Traditional Playwright assertions, focused on individual elements, often lead to flakiness due to race conditions or partial updates. The real challenge is verifying the entire coordinated state is consistent and stable, not just isolated elements.

❌ Relying on page.waitForTimeout() or isolated assertions makes tests brittle. ❌ Missing the "collective harmony" of components leads to false passes or failures.

To architect robust Playwright E2E tests for coordinated UI states, embrace holistic state definition, event-driven waiting, and comprehensive validation.

Here’s how to implement this using page.waitForFunction for true stability:

✅ Define a holistic stable state for your UI. ✅ Use page.waitForFunction to wait for all components to reach that stable state. ✅ Avoid arbitrary waitForTimeout() – wait for explicit signals. ✅ Assert the collective state of interconnected components, not just isolated elements.

Q: Why are traditional Playwright assertions often flaky in complex SPAs? A: They don't account for asynchronous, cascaded updates, leading to assertions on temporary or inconsistent states.

Q: What is the most robust way to wait for UI stability across multiple components? A: Use page.waitForFunction() with a custom JavaScript function that checks for multiple, holistic stability conditions (e.g., absence of all loaders, presence of specific data across elements).

#9723. When I tell Cursor "just make it work", this rule stops the shortcut from rotting

Cursor is very obedient about the word "quick."

If I say "just make it work," it will often make something work by skipping the parts that are annoying: the ownership check, the empty state, the test, the rollback. The feature looks done. A week later I cannot remember which of those shortcuts is load-bearing, and one of them is in a path real users hit.

I got tired of cleaning that up, so I stopped treating "MVP" as a quality setting. I treat it as a scope setting. The rule lives in .cursor/rules/ and I pull it in when I hear myself say "hack this in," "just for now," or "we'll tidy it later."

The useful question is not "how do we write this faster?" It is "what can we not build yet?"

I also tell it what it is not allowed to cut, even in a hurry:

That split is the whole point. "Quick" means the settings UI can wait. It does not mean the webhook can be processed twice.

Some debt is still worth taking. When I take it, I want to find it again on a Monday morning, not rediscover it in production.

This is boring on purpose. The alternative is a vague "we'll refactor this" that nobody can search for.

If I say "prototype" or "throwaway," I want it in /sandbox or on a separate branch, and I want the agent to say out loud that it is not production-safe.

If a real user can reach it, it is production. The "never cut" list applies. Putting a prototype in the same routes as checkout, "just to see," is how a labelled shortcut becomes an unlabelled incident.

Save this as .cursor/rules/60-mvp-not-sloppy.mdc. It is not always-on. It should attach when the task is a prototype, a spike, or a deliberately small first version.

After that I still ask for a short done-summary: what changed, how to verify, and which DEBT(solo) items were added. If the summary has no debt list and the diff quietly skipped a test, the rule did not run.

This is not a substitute for a small-diff rule, a bug-fix playbook, or a real review. It only answers one failure mode: the agent heard "hurry" and lowered the quality bar instead of the feature bar.

If you want the rest of the set I use (core working agreement, feature slicing, root-cause bug fixes, PR review, landing copy), I bundled them as a one-time Cursor pack: shipstack.sognia.workers.dev/cursor-pack. The rule above is usable on its own.

Free sample rule: https://shipstack.sognia.workers.dev/sample

#9722. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.
